tool.name: UV cabinet
tool.measures: the glow of a stone under ultraviolet rays, long-wave (365 nm) and short-wave (254 nm)
tool.where: Gemmology House and Office, bottom row, far left of the laboratory
tips: Switch off the lamp: does the glow stay?

steps.title: An invisible light
steps.text: Beyond violet, there are rays that the eye cannot see: ultraviolet (UV). The cabinet has two lamps: • long-wave UV: 365 nm, the most common; • short-wave UV: 254 nm, more energetic. The cabinet is closed and black: you never look directly at a UV lamp, it harms the eyes.

steps.title: The stone lights up
steps.text: Some stones absorb UV and send it back as visible light, of a longer wavelength: this is fluorescence. In the dark, the stone glows. The colour and strength of the glow depend on the stone: ruby glows red (chromium), some diamonds blue.

steps.title: Two lamps, two answers
steps.text: The same stone can react differently to long-wave and short-wave UV. So you must try both. Example: a natural blue sapphire does not react (or hardly) to UV. A synthetic blue sapphire glows green under short-wave UV, and stays black under long-wave UV. The synthetic blue spinel, for its part, glows red under long-wave UV.

steps.title: Fluorescence or phosphorescence?
steps.text: When the lamp is switched off, fluorescence stops at once. Phosphorescence, on the other hand, goes on: the stone keeps the energy and gives it back slowly, for a few seconds. A natural diamond is rarely phosphorescent. Some synthetic diamonds (HPHT) are: it is a clue.

steps.title: What the cabinet reveals
steps.text: • Ruby, natural or synthetic: red (chromium). • Blue sapphire: natural, nothing; synthetic, green under short-wave UV. • Diamond: variable reaction, from none to strong; blue is the most common. • Fluorite: blue or violet. Pearl: bluish white. • Emerald: red. Kunzite: orange under long-wave UV. • Glass: variable, sometimes a chalky white veil.

steps.title: Using the cabinet
steps.text:
1. Put the stone in the cabinet: it is black.
2. Switch on the long-wave UV lamp, look at the glow.
3. Switch off, then try the short-wave UV.
4. Switch off the lamp and look: does the glow stay?

Each stone glows a little more or less than the average of its species: always compare with a reference stone.

steps.title: To remember
steps.text: • UV makes some stones glow: the colour often says what colours or treats them. • You must try both lamps. • A glow that lasts after switching off is phosphorescence. • The reaction depends on the amount of trace elements, in natural as in synthetic stones: it is an indication, never proof of identity.
